hero.headline: The conversation grows a cockpit
hero.sub: Everything you need to know before you type — how the agent will work, what it is allowed to do, which model is thinking and how hard, and the exact checkout it is standing in — is now one glance above the box.

shot.alt: A fresh chat session in the desktop app: the empty conversation invites you to say something to start, and the composer at the bottom carries the Basic/auto mode trigger, the attach button, the Opus/Xhigh model trigger — with the session's git branch pinned as a chip just above it
shot.caption: A fresh session. Mode, permission, model, effort and the checkout it acts on — all visible before you type a word.

blocks.title: Modes are behaviour, not vibes
blocks.body: Pick how the agent works before it starts, and it actually works that way. Basic is plain Claude. Plan does not write code — it interviews you, and finishes by turning the conversation into a real task you can hand off. Develop builds in waves and has to show you evidence at each one. The same menu holds what the session is allowed to do on its own, and switching either keeps your transcript and whatever you had half-typed. Hand a session off or restart it and it carries its own posture with it: permissions never quietly widen behind your back.

shot.alt: The mode menu open above the composer: Basic selected, Plan ('asks the questions, ends with a task'), Develop ('implements in waves, with evidence'), J.A.R.V.I.S marked SOON, and below a divider the PERMISSION segment with Auto active and Bypass beside it
shot.caption: One menu, both questions: how it works, and what it may do without asking you first.

blocks.title: Choose the brain, and how hard it thinks
blocks.body: Model and reasoning effort finally live in one place, with the real per-token price next to each one so the trade-off is in front of you rather than in a doc. Slide the effort from Low to Max depending on whether this is a gnarly refactor or the tenth small fix today. Found a combination you like? Make it the default and every new session starts there.

shot.alt: The model menu open: Opus marked RECOMMENDED at $5/M in, Sonnet at $3/M in, an OTHER MODELS disclosure, and a REASONING EFFORT slider set to Xhigh with a Set as default button
shot.caption: Opus at Xhigh for the hard refactor, Sonnet at Medium for the everyday loop — one slider apart.

blocks.title: The session tells you where it is standing
blocks.body: The most expensive mistake in an agent session is finding out afterwards that it was working in the wrong place. So the session now says which git checkout it is in, right above the box, and it keeps saying it as the agent moves. Agents can pin more up there: a fact worth keeping in view, or the progress of a task read straight from its own acceptance criteria rather than from a status it typed. The shelf belongs to the composer, so none of it ever scrolls away mid-conversation.

shot.alt: The pinned shelf strip above the composer showing a git branch chip reading feat/chat-checkout-chip-and-fresh-start
shot.caption: The checkout, stated by the session itself — not guessed from what a terminal prompt happens to say.

items.title: You can see what you have left
items.text: A ring on the composer shows how much context this conversation has used, plus your five-hour and weekly limits, read from Claude Code's own numbers. No more discovering the ceiling by hitting it in the middle of something.

items.title: Closing a tab actually closes it
items.text: Closed chat tabs used to leave their Claude process running — roughly 300MB each, stacking up invisibly all day until the machine started to drag. A closed tab now takes its process with it.

items.title: Rename a session where you use it
items.text: Right-click any agent tab to rename it on the spot, and the auto-rename switch that used to be buried three panels deep in Settings is right there with it.

items.title: A worktree has to earn itself
items.text: An agent can only create a second git checkout when the brain is kept separate from the code. Otherwise a project that carries its own memory would end up with two copies of it, drifting apart — which is much harder to notice than it is to cause.

blocks.title: And four that failed without telling you
lines: # A vault whose CHANGELOG was hand-scaffolded as an object, not an array,
# used to pass doctor and return nothing — to the snapshot, and to recall.
✗ core/CHANGELOG.json  wrapper object without an `entries` array
→ 41 entries are being skipped; fix: dreamcontext doctor --fix
# The app-bundled CLI reported 0.0.0, so every version-gated migration
# decided it had nothing to do on the .app's first run. It stamps now.
# `update` exited 0 when it had done nothing at all, so no script could
no supported platform found — nothing to update
# And task-sync pull no longer strips the local-only objectives field:
# 72 task-to-objective links went that way once, reported as success.
✓ 34 pulled · local-only fields preserved · backup written first

blocks.text: All four of those had the same shape: a wrong answer that looked exactly like a right one. Nothing crashed, nothing turned red, and the damage only surfaced weeks later. That is the class of bug this project keeps getting caught by, so they ship alongside the visible work rather than waiting for a quiet release nobody reads.
